bands.name: Govern
bands.rationale: Peaks where data rests and where it is exposed. Little is controllable at origin, and orchestration moves no data values.

bands.name: Quality
bands.rationale: Cheapest to catch early. Peaks at ingest and transform where defects enter or are introduced, and tapers toward the edges.

bands.name: Observe
bands.rationale: Peaks where jobs run and fail, and where spend accrues.

bands.name: Platform
bands.rationale: Environments and workflow matter most where code is written and deployed.

capabilities.description: Can act as the operational system of record behind an application. Scored when the tool is itself such an origin, not when it merely connects to one.

impact.example: A reporting stack reads an application database directly. A schema change in the app breaks reports and nobody planned for it.
impact.matters: The system that creates the data is not in the picture, so how fresh, complete and changeable it is stays a guess.

capabilities.name: Transactional database

capabilities.description: Holds business data in a hosted application and exposes it through an API or export.

impact.example: Sales figures live in a CRM that only exposes a nightly export, so the dashboard is always a day behind.
impact.matters: Business data locked in a hosted application cannot reach the rest of the stack.

capabilities.name: SaaS application data

capabilities.description: Receives or exposes files (CSV, JSON, Parquet, partner extracts) by upload, SFTP or shared storage.

impact.example: A partner emails a spreadsheet each month and someone saves it into a shared folder by hand.
impact.matters: Files from partners and uploads have no agreed place to arrive.

capabilities.name: File drop

capabilities.description: Emits or hosts a continuous feed of application, device or clickstream events.

impact.example: Clickstream data is written to log files and processed once a day, so live features cannot exist.
impact.matters: Continuous events from applications and devices have nothing to publish to or read from.

capabilities.name: Event stream

capabilities.description: Scheduled or on-demand bulk extraction from source systems into the platform.

impact.example: An analyst runs a manual query each morning and pastes the result into the warehouse.
impact.matters: Bulk data cannot be pulled from source systems on a schedule.

capabilities.name: Batch extract

capabilities.description: Log-based or incremental capture of row-level changes from databases.

impact.example: Nightly full copies of a large orders table take six hours and still miss deletions made during the day.
impact.matters: Row-level changes cannot be followed, so copies are either stale or expensive full reloads.

capabilities.name: Change data capture

capabilities.description: Continuous ingestion of event streams with defined delivery semantics.

impact.example: A fraud check runs on data that is an hour old, after the transaction has already cleared.
impact.matters: Events cannot be loaded continuously, so anything needing fresh data waits for the next batch.

capabilities.name: Stream ingest

capabilities.description: Pushing modelled data back into operational and SaaS systems.

impact.example: Analysts compute a churn score, but the sales team cannot see it in their CRM, so it is never used.
impact.matters: Modelled data cannot be pushed back into the tools where people work.

capabilities.name: Reverse ETL

capabilities.description: Durable, cheap, schema-less storage for files and blobs.

impact.example: Raw exports pile up on a file server that runs out of space every quarter.
impact.matters: There is no cheap, durable home for raw files and blobs.

capabilities.name: Object store

capabilities.description: Transactional table layer over files (Iceberg, Delta, Hudi style): ACID, schema evolution, time travel.

impact.example: Two jobs write to the same folder at once and leave half a table behind, with no way to roll back.
impact.matters: Files in the lake have no transactions or history, so concurrent writes corrupt them and mistakes cannot be undone.

capabilities.name: Table format

capabilities.description: Managed analytical store with SQL access, separating modelled data from raw files.

impact.example: Every dashboard queries raw files directly and each one is slow and slightly different.
impact.matters: There is no governed, modelled analytical store behind the reports.

capabilities.name: Warehouse

capabilities.description: Low-latency analytical store built to answer many concurrent aggregate queries.

impact.example: A customer-facing dashboard freezes when fifty people open it at the same time.
impact.matters: Many users or applications cannot get fast answers to aggregate questions at once.

capabilities.name: OLAP serving

capabilities.description: Modelling and reshaping data by authoring SQL.

impact.example: Business logic lives in views edited directly in the console, with no history and no review.
impact.matters: Data cannot be modelled by writing SQL under version control.

capabilities.name: SQL transformation

capabilities.description: Modelling and reshaping data in a general-purpose language (Python, Scala, Spark).

impact.example: A machine-learning preparation step is too complex for SQL and runs by hand on a laptop.
impact.matters: Work that needs a general-purpose language, such as Python or Spark, has nowhere to run.

capabilities.name: Code transformation

capabilities.description: Stateful transformation of events as they arrive: windows, joins, aggregations.

impact.example: A live count of active users has to wait for the nightly batch.
impact.matters: Events cannot be windowed, joined or aggregated as they arrive.

capabilities.name: Stream processing

capabilities.description: Producing, storing and reusing model features, including point-in-time correctness.

impact.example: A model looks great in testing because its features accidentally used data from after the prediction date.
impact.matters: Model features are rebuilt for each project and cannot be reused or made point-in-time correct.

capabilities.name: Feature engineering

capabilities.description: Running work on a time-based schedule.

impact.example: A refresh depends on someone remembering to run it before the Monday meeting.
impact.matters: Work cannot be run on a reliable time-based schedule.

capabilities.name: Scheduling

capabilities.description: Expressing and executing task dependencies, retries and backfills.

impact.example: A report job starts before the load it needs has finished and publishes half-empty numbers.
impact.matters: Tasks cannot be ordered by their dependencies, with retries and backfills.

capabilities.name: Dependency DAG

capabilities.description: Starting work in response to data arrival or external events rather than the clock.

impact.example: A pipeline runs at 6am whether or not the file has landed, and fails on the days it is late.
impact.matters: Work cannot start when data arrives or something happens; it only runs on a clock.

capabilities.name: Event triggers

capabilities.description: Testing and promoting pipeline code and definitions across environments.

impact.example: A fix is copied to production by hand on a Friday and overwrites a colleague's change.
impact.matters: Pipeline changes are not tested and promoted automatically, so they go live by hand.

capabilities.name: CI/CD

capabilities.description: Interactive SQL access for analysts, tools and applications.

impact.example: Analysts request extracts because they cannot query the tables themselves.
impact.matters: Analysts and applications have no interactive SQL access to the data.

capabilities.name: Query engine

capabilities.description: Governed, reusable metric and dimension definitions that sit between data and consumers.

impact.ai: An assistant answering questions in natural language needs governed metric definitions. Without them it invents its own version of revenue.
impact.example: Revenue in the sales dashboard and revenue in the finance report differ by four percent and nobody knows why.
impact.matters: Each tool defines its own metrics, so the same measure differs between dashboards.

capabilities.name: Semantic layer

capabilities.description: Dashboards, reports and exploratory analysis for business users.

impact.example: Managers rely on spreadsheets that analysts refresh by hand.
impact.matters: Business users have no dashboards or reports to explore the data.

capabilities.name: BI and visualisation

capabilities.description: Building interactive applications on top of data.

impact.example: A simple pricing tool needs its own database copy and a separate team to maintain it.
impact.matters: Interactive applications cannot be built on top of the data.

capabilities.name: Data apps

capabilities.description: Deploying trained models and exposing predictions to consumers.

impact.ai: Serving is how model predictions and AI features reach users. Without it a trained model never leaves the notebook.
impact.example: A churn model lives in a notebook, and scores are emailed as a spreadsheet each month.
impact.matters: Trained models cannot be deployed to give predictions to applications.

capabilities.name: ML serving

capabilities.description: Inventory of data assets with ownership, descriptions and search.

impact.ai: An assistant picking tables to answer a question has only names and columns to go on. Without descriptions and owners it guesses, and answers with confidence from the wrong table.
impact.example: Two teams each build a customers table with different definitions. A director sees two revenue figures and nobody can say which is official.
impact.matters: People cannot find the data that exists, or tell which copy to trust, so they rebuild it or use the wrong one.
impact.skip_when: One small team owns every table and can list them from memory.

capabilities.name: Catalog

capabilities.description: Deciding who can read or change which data.

impact.ai: An AI agent acts with the permissions of whoever runs it. Without fine-grained access it can read, summarise and repeat data the person asking was never meant to see.
impact.example: A shared analyst login can read payroll and delete a finance table, and nothing records who did it.
impact.matters: Anyone who can reach the platform can read or change data they should not.
impact.skip_when: A single-user or throwaway stack that holds nothing sensitive.

capabilities.name: Access control

capabilities.description: Obscuring or tokenising sensitive values while keeping data usable.

impact.ai: Models and assistants can memorise and repeat what they read. Masking keeps personal data out of prompts, embeddings and training sets.
impact.example: A developer copies production data into a test schema and now has customers' real phone numbers on their laptop.
impact.matters: Sensitive values such as emails, card numbers and health data are readable in plain text by everyone with access to the table.
impact.skip_when: The data holds no personal, financial or otherwise regulated values.

capabilities.name: Masking

capabilities.description: Defining and enforcing data-handling rules such as retention, residency and classification.

impact.ai: Policy decides what may be used to train or ground a model. Without classification, restricted data can end up in an AI system unnoticed.
impact.example: A rule says customer data must be deleted after twelve months. It is still in three tables, and nobody finds out until an audit.
impact.matters: Rules for keeping, locating and classifying data exist on paper, but nothing enforces them.
impact.skip_when: No retention, residency or classification rules apply to your data.

capabilities.name: Policy

capabilities.description: Assertions on data that pass or fail: uniqueness, nulls, referential integrity, custom rules.

impact.ai: A model cannot tell wrong data from right data. It repeats a bad figure with the same confidence as a good one.
impact.example: A source starts sending nulls in an ID column. A join drops half the orders and the weekly revenue report is quietly 30 percent low.
impact.matters: Bad data reaches dashboards and models before anyone notices, so problems are found from a wrong number.
impact.skip_when: The data is small, hand-checked, and used for exploration rather than decisions.

capabilities.name: Data tests

capabilities.description: Agreed, enforceable schema and semantics at a producer-consumer boundary.

impact.ai: AI applications depend on the shape of the tables they read. A silent schema change can break a feature pipeline or a prompt template without any error.
impact.example: An application team renames a field. The pipeline keeps running, but a downstream metric silently changes meaning.
impact.matters: A change to a source's columns or meaning breaks what is built on it, and the people affected hear last.
impact.skip_when: One team owns both the source and everything downstream of it.

capabilities.name: Data contracts

capabilities.description: Detecting unexpected change in volume, freshness, distribution or schema without hand-written rules.

impact.ai: Stale or drifting data quietly degrades a model's answers, with no error to catch.
impact.example: A feed stops on Friday. Every test still passes because the old rows are fine, and Monday's report shows last week's numbers.
impact.matters: Problems nobody wrote a rule for, such as a sudden drop in volume or a table that stopped updating, go unseen.
impact.skip_when: You have few tables and someone looks at each of them daily.

capabilities.name: Anomaly detection

capabilities.description: Health, freshness and failure visibility, with alerting.

impact.ai: AI features that depend on fresh data fail quietly when a pipeline stalls: the answers just get older.
impact.example: A nightly job fails at 2am. The team learns at 9am when the executive dashboard is empty.
impact.matters: Failures and delays are found by users rather than by the team.
impact.skip_when: Runs are manual and occasional, and watched by the person who starts them.

capabilities.name: Monitoring

capabilities.description: Tracing where data came from and what depends on it.

impact.ai: To trust or audit an AI answer you have to trace it back to the tables and sources it came from. Lineage is the map for that.
impact.example: A team wants to drop a column but cannot tell which dashboards and models use it, so it stays for years.
impact.matters: Nobody can say where a number came from or what breaks when a table changes.
impact.skip_when: You have a handful of tables that one person understands end to end.

capabilities.name: Lineage

capabilities.description: Attributing spend to workloads, teams and datasets.

impact.ai: Embeddings, training runs and model calls can be expensive and bursty, so untracked AI spend grows fast.
impact.example: A misconfigured job scans a large table every hour for a month. The bill triples and finding the cause takes a week.
impact.matters: Spend grows and no one can say which team, job or dataset is causing it.
impact.skip_when: Spend is small and fixed on a flat plan.

capabilities.name: Cost visibility

capabilities.description: Provisioning and running the compute and storage underneath, including infrastructure as code.

impact.ai: Teams add AI services and GPU capacity quickly. Infrastructure defined as code keeps that reviewable and repeatable.
impact.example: Production was set up through a console two years ago. After an accident, nobody can recreate it.
impact.matters: Environments are built by hand, so they drift apart and cannot be rebuilt when something goes wrong.
impact.skip_when: You use a fully managed service where you configure almost nothing.

capabilities.name: Infrastructure

capabilities.description: Separate dev, test and production spaces with safe promotion between them.

impact.ai: Prompts, models and pipelines all need a safe place to be tried before real users and real data see them.
impact.example: A new transformation is run directly against production and overwrites a table that finance depends on.
impact.matters: Changes are tried out on live data because there is nowhere else to test them.
impact.skip_when: It is a single-user project with no shared production.

capabilities.name: Environments

capabilities.description: Tooling that makes authoring, running and debugging work productive: editors, IDEs, local runs, CLIs.

impact.ai: Coding assistants and agents work best with fast local runs, clear errors and text-based definitions. A poor developer loop slows them as much as it slows people.
impact.example: Testing a change means running the whole pipeline in the cloud and waiting an hour, so people avoid touching it.
impact.matters: Building and debugging pipelines is slow and error-prone, so changes are rarer, riskier and rest on a few people.

capabilities.name: Developer experience

roles.description: Moves data between systems: extraction, replication, streaming intake, reverse ETL.
roles.label: Movement

roles.description: Computes over data: warehouses, query engines, general-purpose and streaming compute.
roles.label: Compute

roles.description: Holds data: operational databases, object stores, table formats, the layer underneath.
roles.label: Storage

roles.description: Reshapes data into modelled datasets: SQL transformation and feature engineering.
roles.label: Modelling

roles.description: Decides when and in what order work runs, and how changes are shipped.
roles.label: Orchestration

roles.description: Controls who can see and do what: catalogs, access control, masking, policy.
roles.label: Governance

roles.description: Watches the data and the system: quality checks, monitoring, lineage, cost.
roles.label: Monitoring

roles.description: Where people and applications meet the data: BI, apps, semantic layers, IDEs, ML endpoints.
roles.label: Consumption

stages.description: Where data originates: the operational systems, applications and feeds that produce it.
stages.name: Source
stages.rationale: The systems data comes from usually sit outside the stack, so having no source tool is normal and never a gap.

stages.description: Moving data from sources into the platform.

impact.ai: An assistant or model answers from whatever was last loaded. If loading is manual, its answers are as old as the last upload.
impact.example: Someone exports a CSV from the CRM every Monday and pastes it into the warehouse. When they are away, every report stays a week out of date.
impact.matters: Data reaches the platform late, by hand, or not at all.
impact.skip_when: Your platform reads from the source systems directly, or the data already lives inside it.

stages.name: Ingest
stages.rationale: Data has to arrive somewhere, though a stack that works inside its own platform can do without.

stages.description: Where data rests and how it is laid out for analytical use.

impact.ai: Models and retrieval systems need a governed, queryable copy to read from. Without one they are fed files that nobody owns.
impact.example: Results live in spreadsheets and one analyst's laptop. When the laptop is replaced, three months of history goes with it.
impact.matters: There is nowhere durable and queryable to keep the data, so it is recomputed, lost or scattered.
impact.skip_when: Nothing you build needs to keep data; everything is read live from the source.

stages.name: Store
stages.rationale: Nothing works without somewhere to keep the data.

stages.description: Reshaping raw data into modelled, trustworthy datasets.

impact.ai: A model trained or prompted on raw data learns its mistakes, duplicates and quirks as if they were facts.
impact.example: Two dashboards define an active customer differently, so the same question gets two answers in the same meeting.
impact.matters: Raw data is used as it arrives, so every analyst cleans and interprets it their own way.
impact.skip_when: Reporting is simple and reads clean tables straight from a system that already models them.

stages.name: Transform
stages.rationale: Raw data is rarely fit to use, though simple reporting can skip it.

stages.description: Deciding when work runs, in what order, and how changes are shipped.

impact.ai: Retrieval indexes, feature tables and model refreshes need to run on time and in order. Without scheduling they drift out of date silently.
impact.example: A nightly refresh is a script on a colleague's laptop. It stops on the day they go on leave and no one notices for a week.
impact.matters: Work starts by hand or from scripts on someone's machine, so it stops when they do and nothing ships safely.
impact.skip_when: The work is run rarely and on purpose, by the person who wrote it.

stages.name: Orchestrate
stages.rationale: Work can be started by hand or by scripts, which is painful but not fatal.

stages.description: Getting data to the people, applications and models that use it.

impact.ai: This is where AI meets the data: assistants that answer questions, applications that retrieve from it, models that predict from it. Without a serving layer the pipeline's value never reaches them.
impact.example: The warehouse is full of clean tables, but the business still asks for spreadsheets because there is no way to explore them.
impact.matters: Nobody outside the pipeline can use the result: no dashboards, applications or models consume the data.
impact.skip_when: The output is a file or feed that another system collects, so this stack has no consumers of its own.

stages.name: Serve
stages.rationale: Data nobody can reach has no value.
